local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 Utah's counties elect the county officers whose four-year terms end this year (as a rule, commission or council seats and the county clerk, auditor, sheriff and attorney), local school boards elect about half their members, special districts on the even-year cycle fill board seats, and justice court judges whose terms end face a yes or no retention vote. City and town offices, and special districts on the municipal cycle, are elected in November of odd-numbered years, next in 2027. The county treasurer, recorder, surveyor and assessor are, as a rule, on the other four-year cycle, next in 2028.
local_calendar.s: Utah Code 20A-1-201 and 20A-1-202 (what each November election fills), 17-66-202 (county officers' terms), 20A-14-202 (local school boards), 17B-1-306 (special districts) and 78A-7-203 (justice court judges)

local_coverage.t: Loaded for Utah's local level so far: the justice court judges' retention questions on the Lieutenant Governor's amended General Election Certification (30 of them, for county and city courts alike), filed with the other judges and tied to the counties where those courts sit (17 of the 29). County offices and local school board contests, from each county clerk's own list (Utah has no statewide list of them), are loaded for 6 of the 29 counties: Salt Lake County (26 contests), Utah County (13 contests), Davis County (10 contests), Weber County (14 contests), Washington County (9 contests) and Cache County (19 contests). Cache County's list also carries the Cache Water District's board seats, which are loaded with them. Not loaded yet: the other 23 counties' lists, and special district boards elsewhere. Ballot questions are not loaded: the proposed constitutional amendments and local propositions.

measures.t: Proposal to Amend Utah Constitution - Publication Amendments
measures.q:
Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers?
If voters approve Constitutional Amendment A, state statute would change to require the Lieutenant Governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments and other ballot questions from the Legislature, on the Utah Public Notice Website and on the Lieutenant Governor’s website for 60 days immediately before the general election.
measures.s:
Current Provisions of the Utah Constitution
Under the Utah Constitution, the Legislature may propose a constitutional amendment with a two-thirds vote in each house. The proposed amendment is then submitted to voters at a general election for approval or rejection.
Before the election, the Constitution requires the Legislature to publish the proposed amendment in a newspaper in each county for two months.
Effect of Constitutional Amendment A
Constitutional Amendment A would require publication of a proposed constitutional amendment for 60 calendar days immediately before the general election in a manner set by state law rather than requiring publication in newspapers for two months immediately before the general election.
Constitutional Amendment A would not change how constitutional amendments are proposed or approved by voters.
Implementing Legislation
If voters approve Constitutional Amendment A, H.B. 481, Ballot Proposition Requirements, enacted during the 2025 General Session, will take effect. H.B. 481 requires the Lieutenant Governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments and other ballot questions from the Legislature, on the Utah Public Notice Website and on the Lieutenant Governor’s website for 60 calendar days immediately before the general election.
measures.sb: The presiding officers of the Legislature: the "Impartial Analysis" in the Lieutenant Governor's 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet, which says the presiding officers write the analysis of each measure. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.f: If approved, Constitutional Amendment A, together with H.B. 481, could reduce state costs by up to $1.4 million every two years, based on recent estimates. The savings from changing the publication requirement for proposed constitutional amendments from newspapers to publicly operated websites would vary depending on the length of each proposed constitutional amendment and newspaper publication rates.
measures.fb: The "Fiscal Effects" section of the Voter Information Pamphlet, which says the presiding officers of the Legislature prepare the fiscal impact estimate. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more YES votes than NO votes among the voters who vote on it. (Utah Constitution, article XXIII, section 1; H.J.R. 10, section 3)
measures.h: Proposed by the Legislature in House Joint Resolution 10 of the 2025 General Session, passed 29 to 0 in the Senate and 70 to 0 in the House, with 5 members not present. A Utah amendment needs the votes of two thirds of all members elected to each house before it goes to the voters. (Utah Constitution, article XXIII, section 1)
measures.nt: The ballot title is drafted by the Office of Legislative Research and General Counsel, as the pamphlet says. The pamphlet prints both paragraphs of the question under "Ballot Title"; the second says what state law will do if the amendment passes. If approved, the amendment takes effect on January 1, 2027. Because the Legislature adopted it unanimously, the pamphlet prints an argument in favor and no argument against.

measures.t: Proposal to Amend Utah Constitution - Statewide Initiatives
measures.q: Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to require that citizen-proposed laws that increase taxes compared to existing law be approved by at least 60% of voters, instead of a simple majority?
measures.s:
Current Constitutional Provision
The Utah Constitution allows voters to propose and pass a state law through a statewide initiative. Statewide initiatives are voted on by the people, and most are approved if a majority (more than half) of voters approve the measure; however, statewide initiatives related to the taking of wildlife require approval by two-thirds of voters.
Effect of Constitutional Amendment B
Constitutional Amendment B would increase the voter approval required for statewide initiatives that increase taxes compared to existing law.
Statewide initiatives voted on after November 1, 2026, would require approval by at least 60% of voters if the statewide initiative:
Creates a new tax;
Expands an existing tax to cover additional items or transactions;
Increases an existing tax rate; or
Changes a property tax rate in a way that results in a smaller decrease in the property tax rate than would occur under existing law.
Constitutional Amendment B would not change the vote required to approve any other type of statewide initiative.
measures.sb: The presiding officers of the Legislature: the "Impartial Analysis" in the Lieutenant Governor's 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet, which says the presiding officers write the analysis of each measure. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.f: Enactment of Constitutional Amendment B likely would not materially impact current state revenues or expenditures.
measures.fb: The "Fiscal Effects" section of the Voter Information Pamphlet, which says the presiding officers of the Legislature prepare the fiscal impact estimate. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more YES votes than NO votes among the voters who vote on it. Its own 60 percent rule would apply only to later initiatives, not to this question. (Utah Constitution, article XXIII, section 1; S.J.R. 2, section 3)
measures.h: Proposed by the Legislature in Senate Joint Resolution 2 of the 2025 General Session, passed 21 to 8 in the Senate and 55 to 17 in the House, with 3 members not present. A Utah amendment needs the votes of two thirds of all members elected to each house before it goes to the voters. (Utah Constitution, article XXIII, section 1)

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Utah Office of the Lieutenant Governor’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the June 23 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, county offices are elected on party lines; school districts and other districts are nonpartisan. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (June 23) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau, the Cache County Clerk/Auditor, the Salt Lake County Clerk, the Davis County Clerk/Auditor, the Utah County Clerk, the Weber County Clerk/Auditor and the Washington County Clerk/Auditor, each named among these sources; where something on a county’s ballot could not be shown, that county’s page says what and why.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the Utah Geospatial Resource Center and Utah Lieutenant Governor's Office and the U.S. Census Bureau: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For statewide offices, the Legislature, judges, county offices and school boards a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Candidates for soil and water, hospital and other small district boards show what they filed and, if they listed one, their campaign website. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: the official precinct results, added up here by county and district on the lines in force at that election; the results read here give no figures for a city or town, and the page says so there. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from your precinct, where the map files place it, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

county_commissioner.t: The county's governing board passes the budget, sets taxes and oversees services like roads. Its members are called commissioners, and in some places supervisors or police jurors.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-11, Board of County Commissioners, North Dakota Legislative Branch
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: La junta de gobierno del condado aprueba el presupuesto, fija los impuestos y supervisa servicios como los caminos. Sus miembros se llaman comisionados y, en algunos lugares, supervisores o jurados de policía.

county_council.t: The county council makes the county's laws. A separate elected executive or mayor runs the county's departments.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives
Maryland Constitution, Article XI-A, Maryland State Archives

x.es: El concejo del condado hace las leyes del condado. Un ejecutivo o un alcalde elegido por separado dirige los departamentos del condado.

county_executive.t: This office runs the county's offices, while a separate elected council makes the laws. In Kentucky the county judge/executive also leads the county board.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives
Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: Este cargo dirige las oficinas del condado, mientras que un concejo elegido por separado hace las leyes. En Kentucky, el juez/ejecutivo del condado también dirige la junta del condado.

court_of_appeals.t: The court of appeals is the middle level of state courts. Its judges check trial court rulings for legal mistakes when one side appeals, and they do not hold new trials.
s: Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
How courts work, California Courts Self-Help Center
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice

x.es: El tribunal de apelaciones es el nivel intermedio de los tribunales del estado. Cuando una de las partes apela, sus jueces revisan si las decisiones de los tribunales de primera instancia tienen errores legales, y no celebran juicios nuevos.

district_attorney.t: The district attorney is the prosecutor for a county or a group of counties. The office brings criminal cases for the state and argues them in court.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 5 (Judicial Department), Texas Legislature
Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 8, ORS 8.660, Attending court and prosecuting offenses, Oregon Legislature

x.es: El fiscal de distrito es el fiscal de un condado o de un grupo de condados. La oficina presenta casos penales en nombre del estado y los argumenta ante el tribunal.

district_court.t: In most of these states the district court is the main trial court, where most cases start. In Alabama, Michigan, Washington, New York and a few other states it is a lower court for minor crimes, traffic and small lawsuits.

En Alabama, Michigan, Washington, Nueva York y algunos otros estados, es un tribunal inferior para delitos menores, casos de tránsito y demandas pequeñas.

justice_court.t: Justice courts are local courts of a town, village, city or county. They handle traffic tickets, minor crimes and small claims.
s: The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State
An Overview of the Utah Justice Courts, Utah State Courts

x.es: Los tribunales de paz son tribunales locales de un pueblo, una villa, una ciudad o un condado. Atienden multas de tránsito, delitos menores y reclamos menores.

juvenile_court.t: A juvenile court hears cases about children. These include young people charged with breaking the law and children who may be harmed or neglected.
s: State and Local Government, Chapter 1 Part B: The Judicial Branch, Louisiana House of Representatives
Guide to the Courts, Utah State Courts
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch

x.es: Un tribunal de menores atiende casos sobre niños. Estos incluyen a jóvenes acusados de violar la ley y a niños que pueden haber sufrido daño o descuido.

school_board.t: The school board runs a public school district. It hires the superintendent, sets district rules, passes the budget and, in many states, sets the local school tax.
s: Statutory Requirements for School Districts, Informational Paper 29 (Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau), Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction

x.es: La junta escolar dirige un distrito escolar público. Contrata al superintendente, fija las reglas del distrito, aprueba el presupuesto y, en muchos estados, fija el impuesto escolar local.

sheriff.t: In most states the sheriff is the county's top law officer. The office keeps the peace, runs the jail and carries out court orders; in Kentucky it also collects property taxes.
s: Minnesota Statutes 387.03, Powers, duties, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Minnesota Statutes 387.11, County jail, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el alguacil es el principal agente de la ley del condado. La oficina mantiene la paz, dirige la cárcel y cumple las órdenes de los tribunales; en Kentucky, también cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad.

state_board_of_education.t: The state board of education sets rules for public schools across the state. These cover what students should learn, what they need to graduate, and in Texas, textbooks too.
s: SBOE Homepage, Texas State Board of Education
State Board, Kansas State Department of Education
Texas Education Code, Chapter 7 (State Board of Education powers and duties), Texas Legislature
Texas Education Code, Chapter 31 (instructional materials), Texas Legislature

x.es: La junta estatal de educación fija reglas para las escuelas públicas de todo el estado. Estas reglas abarcan lo que los estudiantes deben aprender, lo que necesitan para graduarse y, en Texas, también los libros de texto.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

x.es: La Cámara de Representantes del estado (llamada Asamblea o Cámara de Delegados en algunos estados) es la cámara más grande. Sus miembros redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

supreme_court.t: The state supreme court is the state's highest court. It hears appeals from lower courts and has the final say on state law (Texas also has a top court for criminal cases).
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Judicial System Structure, Supreme Court of Ohio

x.es: La corte suprema del estado es el tribunal más alto del estado. Atiende apelaciones de los tribunales inferiores y tiene la última palabra sobre la ley estatal (Texas también tiene un tribunal máximo para los casos penales).

water_board.t: Water district board members run a public district that supplies water, and in some places sewer service or farm water, to its area. They set its rates and budget.
s: What's So Special About Special Districts? (4th ed.), California Senate Local Government Committee

x.es: Los miembros de la junta de un distrito de suministro de agua dirigen un distrito público que suministra agua a su zona y, en algunos lugares, servicio de alcantarillado o agua para la agricultura. Fijan sus tarifas y su presupuesto.
